title: Children of the resurrection (Luke 20:20–40)
hookLine: trick questions about taxes and the dead: for all live to him

lines: A QUESTION WHERE EVERY ANSWER LOSES.
WHOSE PICTURE IS ON THE COIN?
A SECOND TRAP, ABOUT THE DEAD.
cards: A trick question is built so every answer loses. Luke says the leaders now send spies who pretend to be sincere: is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not? Say yes, and the crowd hears a man who bows to Rome.
Say no, and Rome hears a rebel. Jesus asks whose picture is on a coin. Caesar's.

Then, in the King James Bible: "Render therefore unto Caesar the things which be Caesar's, and unto God the things which be God's." They go quiet. Then a second group arrives with a second trap, this one about the dead.

teach.b: They're Sadducees, and Luke tells us they deny any resurrection. So they spin a story to make it look ridiculous. Moses taught that if a man dies without children, his brother should marry the widow.
Seven brothers, one after another, marry the same woman, and each dies. In the resurrection, whose wife will she be? Jesus doesn't laugh at them.
He says the life to come isn't a copy of this one. People there don't marry, because they can't die any more.
They are, in the King James words, "the children of God, being the children of the resurrection." That's a Hebrew way of speaking: a child of something belongs to it, and its life is shaped by it.

teach.h: THE GOD OF ABRAHAM, ISAAC AND JACOB.
teach.b: Then Jesus goes back to Moses, to the burning bush, where God calls himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, long after all three had died. Not the God they used to have. Their God, now.
And today's line: "For he is not a God of the dead, but of the living: for all live unto him."

In this argument Jesus stands on the same side as the Pharisees, who also taught the resurrection, and some of the scribes answer, "Master, thou hast well said." After that, nobody dares ask him anything.
At funerals, some Christians hear in all live to him a promise about the people they've lost: not gone from God, even when gone from us.

how: Some churches read Jesus's answer to the Sadducees at funerals or on All Souls' Day, and some remember their dead by name in worship.

games.q: what's inside Luke 20:20–40 — tap the pairs.
p: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob

s: he answers it seriously, and goes back to Moses and the burning bush.
Jesus says the risen marry just as people do now
he says they neither marry nor can die, because they are children of the resurrection.

games.q: you're asked: is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar? yes angers the crowd, no angers Rome. what do you do?
o: say yes, and keep Rome happy.
say no, and win the crowd.
ask whose picture is on the coin.
games.why: he asks for a coin, then says: "render therefore unto Caesar the things which be Caesar's, and unto God the things which be God's."

practice: Bring to mind one person you've lost, a grandparent, a friend, a teacher, even a pet if that's where your heart goes, and let their face or voice come near for a minute; you don't have to feel anything big.
If you pray, say their name to God with Jesus' words, all live unto him. If not, hold them with gratitude and whatever hope you have.

wordCard.voice: Sadducees, the group who denied any resurrection and tried to trap Jesus with a riddle about seven brothers and one widow.

orig.note: Greek: sons of the resurrection. a Semitic idiom: a 'son of' something belongs to it or shares its nature.

carryVoice: Your line: all live to him. Words to keep close on hard days. That's day five hundred seventy-three.
